title: Health Assessment & Nursing Skills: Respiratory Assessment—Inspection, Auscultation & Early Deterioration
html:
A respiratory assessment determines whether the client can maintain a patent airway, move air effectively, exchange gases, clear secretions, and tolerate activity. The RN combines what the client reports with work of breathing, respiratory pattern, mental status, skin and mucosal findings, chest movement, lung sounds, oxygen delivery, pulse oximetry, vital-sign trends, and change from baseline. No isolated number or sound replaces the whole clinical picture.

Learning goals

  • Collect a focused respiratory history and identify time-sensitive symptoms.
  • Inspect respiratory rate, pattern, effort, speech, position, color, and chest symmetry.
  • Palpate the chest and compare expansion when appropriate.
  • Auscultate lung fields directly on the skin using a reproducible side-to-side pattern.
  • Describe expected, diminished, and adventitious breath sounds without overdiagnosing.
  • Recognize deterioration, escalate promptly, and document the response.

Start with the airway and the client—not the stethoscope

Observe before directing the client’s breathing. Can the client speak normally? Is the airway open? Note voice change, drooling, choking, inability to handle secretions, noisy upper-airway breathing, position, facial expression, level of consciousness, and visible distress. Severe dyspnea, stridor, cyanosis, sudden inability to speak, markedly reduced air movement, or declining responsiveness requires immediate airway and breathing support and the appropriate emergency response.

A quieter chest is not always improvement
Wheezing that becomes faint while effort, fatigue, mental status, or oxygenation worsens may mean very little air is moving. Treat the entire pattern as deterioration rather than assuming the obstruction has resolved.

Ask a focused respiratory history

Clarify onset, duration, pattern, progression, and triggers of shortness of breath. Ask whether symptoms occur at rest, with activity, when lying flat, at night, or with exposure. Explore cough, sputum amount and appearance, blood, chest discomfort, fever or chills, wheezing, noisy breathing, sleep interruption, fatigue, reduced activity, recent illness or procedures, aspiration risk, sick contacts, travel or environmental and occupational exposures when relevant.

Review respiratory diagnoses, prior exacerbations or hospitalizations, allergies, prescribed inhalers or nebulizers, recent medication response, home oxygen or positive-airway-pressure use, and the client’s usual oxygen saturation and activity tolerance when known. Ask about tobacco, vaping, cannabis, and other inhaled substances in neutral language; include amount, duration, recent change, and interest in support without stigma. New hemoptysis, sudden pleuritic pain with dyspnea, or rapidly worsening symptoms requires prompt evaluation rather than completion of every routine question.

Inspect the respiratory pattern

Count respirations while the client is at rest and preferably before calling attention to the count, because conscious control can change the pattern. Observe rate, rhythm, depth, and effort. Count for the interval required by the clinical situation and policy; use a full minute when the pattern is irregular or accuracy is especially important. Interpret the finding with age, sleep or activity, pain, anxiety, fever, medications, neurologic status, and baseline.

Look for accessory-muscle use, intercostal or suprasternal retractions, nasal flaring, pursed-lip breathing, tripod positioning, paradoxical movement, inability to lie flat, and pauses in breathing. Note whether the client speaks in full sentences or only short phrases, and whether movement or conversation worsens symptoms. Inspect chest shape and bilateral expansion, tracheal position when indicated, cough strength, and the ability to clear secretions.

Assess color using more than one site and never rely on skin color alone. Pallor or cyanosis may be easier to recognize in lips, tongue, oral mucosa, conjunctivae, nail beds, palms, or soles depending on pigmentation and perfusion. Compare with baseline and pair color findings with mental status, respiratory effort, pulse oximetry quality, and circulation.

Palpate and percuss purposefully

With consent, palpate for chest tenderness, temperature, masses, or crepitus and compare posterior chest expansion when appropriate. New crepitus, asymmetric expansion, pain, or instability is a cue for focused assessment and escalation based on context. Do not repeatedly press a painful or injured area simply to reproduce a finding.

Percussion may help identify differences in underlying density when it is part of the trained examination. Compare side to side at corresponding landmarks. A localized dull or hyperresonant note is a clue—not a diagnosis—and must be interpreted with symptoms, inspection, palpation, auscultation, vital signs, and diagnostic data.

Auscultate in a side-to-side ladder

Use the diaphragm of the stethoscope directly on skin in a quiet environment. Position the client upright when tolerated; if positioning is limited, document the areas assessed and the limitation. Ask for slow, slightly deeper breaths through an open mouth, pausing if the client becomes dizzy, fatigued, increasingly dyspneic, or unable to continue.

Listen to one complete inspiratory-expiratory cycle at each site. Compare corresponding right and left areas from apices toward bases, avoiding bone and breast tissue when possible. Assess posterior, lateral, and anterior fields as the condition and setting require. Do not auscultate only the symptomatic side: comparison helps identify regional change.

Describe sounds before explaining them

  • Expected breath sounds: vesicular, bronchovesicular, and bronchial sounds occur over characteristic locations. A normally soft sound can be abnormal if heard in the wrong place.
  • Diminished or absent sounds: may reflect reduced airflow, obstruction, air or fluid around the lung, consolidation, body habitus, shallow effort, or technique. Reposition or validate technique when safe, then act on the complete pattern.
  • Crackles: discontinuous popping sounds, often heard during inspiration. Describe location, timing, extent, and change rather than assuming one cause.
  • Wheezes: musical sounds associated with narrowed airways. Note whether they are localized or diffuse and inspiratory or expiratory.
  • Rhonchi or coarse sounds: lower-pitched continuous sounds that may occur with secretions in larger airways; note whether coughing changes the sound.
  • Stridor: a harsh upper-airway sound that can signal critical obstruction and requires immediate assessment.
  • Pleural friction rub: a grating sound associated with pleural surfaces moving against each other; correlate with pain and other findings.

Never document “lungs clear” if only one small area was heard. Specify where sounds were assessed, their intensity and character, whether findings were bilateral, and any conditions that limited the examination.

Interpret oxygen and monitoring data in context

Identify whether the client is on room air or receiving oxygen. If oxygen is prescribed, document the device, flow rate or ordered concentration, fit, tubing connections, skin condition, and the client’s response. Compare with the prescribed target and the client’s baseline. Do not change oxygen outside orders, protocols, or emergency authority; do not remove oxygen simply to obtain an untreated reading when doing so could be unsafe.

Pulse oximetry estimates arterial oxygen saturation but does not measure ventilation or carbon dioxide. Validate a reading that conflicts with the client by checking the waveform or signal, sensor placement, movement, perfusion, ambient light, nail products when relevant, and equipment function. A reassuring number does not cancel severe work of breathing, altered mental status, or poor air movement. A concerning number with distress warrants action while measurement quality is assessed.

Recognize deterioration as a cluster

High-risk clusters include increased work of breathing plus falling saturation; new confusion or somnolence plus shallow respirations; stridor plus voice change; unilateral diminished sounds plus sudden pain or procedural history; new crackles plus increasing oxygen requirement; or fatigue with decreasing air movement. Prioritize airway, breathing, circulation, and neurologic status. Position the client to support ventilation when appropriate, ensure prescribed oxygen delivery is intact, obtain assistance, initiate authorized interventions, and communicate the trend and baseline change.

After intervention, reassess the same clinically important measures: airway sound, respiratory rate and effort, ability to speak, lung sounds, oxygen device and setting, saturation and signal quality, mental status, comfort, and activity tolerance. Improvement in only one value is not enough if other signs worsen.

Document observations, context, action, and response

Record symptoms in the client’s own words when useful; onset and provoking factors; respiratory rate, rhythm, depth, and effort; speech and position; chest symmetry; cough and sputum characteristics; lung-sound location and character; oxygen device and setting; pulse-oximetry reading and conditions; comparison with baseline; focused follow-up; interventions; notification; and reassessment.

For example: “1410: New dyspnea at rest; speaking in three- to four-word phrases, RR 30/min with accessory-muscle use. Breath sounds diminished at right base compared with left; SpO₂ 89% with consistent waveform on prescribed nasal cannula 2 L/min. High Fowler position; tubing and device checked; rapid response activated at 1412. At 1420, team at bedside; client alert, RR 26/min, oxygen managed per response-team orders.” The entry reports what was observed and done without substituting an unconfirmed diagnosis.

Clinical example

A client with a history of asthma initially has diffuse wheezing. Ten minutes later, the wheeze is barely audible, but the client is drowsy, breathing shallowly, and no longer able to speak. The RN recognizes that reduced sound with worsening effort and mental status may reflect critically reduced airflow, initiates immediate airway and breathing support, activates the emergency response, and continues reassessment rather than charting “wheezing improved.”
